title: Refocusing Mammalian Synbio to Speak the Language of Biology (and Improve Human Health)
speaker: Ron Weiss
content: Synthetic biology is revolutionizing how we conceptualize and approach the engineering of biological systems. Recent advances in the field are allowing us to expand beyond the construction and analysis of small gene networks towards the implementation of complex multicellular systems with a variety of applications. In this talk I will describe our integrated computational / experimental approach to engineering complex behavior in a variety of cells, with a focus on mammalian cells. In our research, we appropriate design principles from electrical engineering and other established fields.
rawEventDetails: Speaker Ron Weiss Affiliation Massachusetts Institute of Technology Details Event Description Synthetic biology is revolutionizing how we conceptualize and approach the engineering of biological systems. Recent advances in the field are allowing us to expand beyond the construction and analysis of small gene networks towards the implementation of complex multicellular systems with a variety of applications. In this talk I will describe our integrated computational / experimental approach to engineering complex behavior in a variety of cells, with a focus on mammalian cells. In our research, we appropriate design principles from electrical engineering and other established fields. These principles include abstraction, standardization, modularity, and computer aided design. But we also spend considerable effort towards understanding what makes synthetic biology different from all other existing engineering disciplines and discovering new design and construction rules that are effective for this unique discipline. We will briefly describe the implementation of genetic circuits and modules with finely-tuned digital, analog, and multicellular behavior. We will also discuss the generation of a complex tissue from human induced pluripotent stem cells that recapitulates early developmental processes and exhibits a liver bud-like phenotype with integrated vasculature that can be used for drug development and potentially for tissue transplantation. Finally, we will present a mechanism for creation of artificial neural networks that operate in cells using translational regulation, providing a finely tuned mechanism for obtaining non-binary, non-monotonic behaviors with precise amplitude and temporal dynamics and paving the way for cells that can be trained and autonomously learn to perform specific behavioral tasks. Refreshments will be available 15 minutes prior to the start of the seminar. Sponsor Omenn Darling Bioengineering Institute

rawEventDetails: Speaker Mattia Serra Affiliation University of California, San Diego Details Event Description Embryonic tissues undergo coordinated flows during avian gastrulation to establish the body plan. Here, we elucidate how tens of thousands of cells coordinate their behaviors to sculpt the chick embryo’s dynamic geometry (size and shape). Each of these two distinct geometric changes is associated with dynamic curves across which trajectories separate (kinematic repellers). Through physical modeling and experimental manipulations, we selectively eliminate either or both repellers in model and experiments, revealing their mechanistic origins. We find that embryo size is affected by the competition between extraembryonic epiboly and embryonic myosin-driven contraction—which persists even when mesoderm induction is blocked. Instead, the characteristic shape change from circular to pear-shaped arises from myosin-driven cell intercalations in the mesendoderm, irrespective of epiboly. These findings elucidate modular mechanisms that independently regulate embryo size and shape during development. Refreshments available 15 minutes before indicated time of seminar

rawEventDetails: Speaker Aditya Raguram Affiliation Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research Details Event Description The ability to deliver proteins and RNAs into cells within the body is required for many emerging therapeutic modalities, including gene editing therapies, but efficient intracellular macromolecular delivery remains challenging. To address this challenge, we developed engineered virus-like particles (eVLPs): intracellular delivery vehicles that use retroviral scaffold proteins to package and deliver cargo proteins or RNAs instead of viral genetic material. We used protein engineering and capsid evolution to generate eVLPs that mediate highly efficient gene editing in mice and primary human cells. Additionally, we developed a genome-wide screening approach to systematically investigate how genetic perturbations in producer cells influence eVLP production, and we used this approach to engineer producer cells that support improved particle production and cargo delivery. Overall, eVLPs combine key advantages of both viral and non-viral delivery strategies and are promising tools for therapeutic gene editing, functional genomics, and disease modeling. rawEventDetails: Speakers Carsen Stringer Affiliation HHMI Janelia Research Campus Marius Pachitariu Affiliation HHMI Janelia Research Campus Details Event Description AI-based methods for biological data analysis Machine learning methods are increasingly necessary to analyze biological datasets as they become larger and larger, but traditional AI methods are not designed for biology problems. My lab develops AI methods for analyzing and understanding large-scale biological data. We focus on multiple problems in visual-based segmentation and tracking, as well as on predictive models of neural activity with an emphasis on interpretability. I will present two of our long-term projects, one in the area of cellular and subcellular segmentation and one in the area of behavioral-to-neural predictive models. We have developed a widely used deep learning-based bioimage analysis package called Cellpose, which can denoise, deconvolve, upscale and segment arbitrary repeating elements in an image, most commonly cells. I will present our current efforts to increase segmentation quality for 3D and live-cell imaging. Using a model called Facemap, I will show that we can predict the mind of a mouse from its face, and discuss what this means for understanding neuronal dynamics. Visual learning in biological neural networks Biological intelligence has an unmatched capacity to solve problems arising in new situations not previously encountered. This capacity arises from many layers of previous experience and learning throughout the lifetime, which modifies synaptic circuits in the brain and changes neural network representations. My lab studies the nature of these changes in visual cortical circuits, and how the neuronal changes affect behavior in novel scenarios. Using large-scale neural recordings across a majority of visual cortical areas in mice, we found that visual experience during development is necessary to establish invariant visual representations. We also found that visual experience in adulthood reorganizes representations in most visual cortical areas, enables faster subsequent learning and accounts for a substantial portion of all plasticity observed during sensorimotor learning. Additional representational changes were induced by learned behavior in higher-order visual areas. I will also describe planned future work for identifying the anatomical substrates of this representational plasticity, and the mathematical hypotheses we have for interpreting the anatomical and functional data. Refreshments will be available 15 minutes prior to the start of the seminar. Sponsors Omenn-Darling Bioengineering Institute Princeton Neuroscience Institute

title: Extensive Gene Evolution on Laboratory Timescales
speaker: Chang Liu
content: My group engineers genetic systems that accelerate the speed of gene evolution in vivo, enabling us to discover new biomolecular functions and explore sequence-to-function relationships at scale. I will summarize our development of orthogonal DNA replication (OrthoRep) to drive experimental evolution of chosen genes at 1-million times the genomic error rate. I will present applications OrthoRep to studying and engineering enzymes, antibodies, and arbitrary genes.Refreshments will be available 15 minutes prior to the start of the seminar.

rawEventDetails: Speaker Lulu Qian Affiliation California Institute of Technology Details Event Description Intelligence has traditionally been discussed at the level of organisms and, increasingly, cells. Yet rudimentary forms of intelligence could exist at the molecular level—not in individual molecules, but in systems of molecules that interact, change, remember, and persist together. Can a molecular system recognize high-dimensional patterns? Can it observe molecular examples of stimuli paired with desired responses, generalize learned patterns, and respond appropriately to new variations of the stimuli on its own? Can sophisticated information processing and learning arise from pure nucleic-acid systems, without complex proteins or enzymatic pathways? Can long-term learning and evolutionary behavior be powered by an environmental energy source, using a rudimentary metabolism far simpler than modern biology? In this talk, I will provide concrete evidence for some aspects of these questions and speculate on the others. Light Refreshments will be available 15 minutes prior to the start of the seminar. Sponsor Omenn-Darling Bioengineering Institute

rawEventDetails: Speaker Tobin Sosnick Affiliation University of Chicago Details Event Description Hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) reveals that proteins constantly undergo local unfolding events, ranging from small fluctuations to large-scale openings, that transiently break backbone hydrogen bonds. The measured exchange rates report on the stability and folding cooperativity of individual protein segments. We propose that cooperative unfolding regions correspond to mechanically stiff elements that can transmit force or store strain energy. In contrast, regions of low cooperativity correspond to flexible elements that can optimize binding interfaces and enable rapid motions. This interpretation rationalizes functional data across a diverse array of systems. In the second part, we characterize the hydrogen bond network and condensation of yeast Pab1, a stress granule marker that, unlike proteins that undergo reversible liquid-liquid phase separation, condenses irreversibly. We propose a sequential activation model in which each of four RRM domains activates at progressively higher temperatures, partially unfolds, and associates with other activated RRMs. Our latest results reveal that three regions within the RRM domains form amyloidogenic latches that account for the condensate's irreversibility. Refreshments will be available 15 minutes prior to the start of the seminar. Sponsor Omenn-Darling Bioengineering Institute
